quirks: Civil marriage registration in Saratoga County/New York State did not begin until 1880, so a marriage in the requested 1855-1864 window will not be in state vital records — rely instead on church registers, the 1855/1865/1875 NY State Census marriage schedules, and county clerk marriage license records if filed.

For an Irish Catholic couple, no tool result in this survey names the specific Catholic parish serving Saratoga County in this period; parishes fall under the Diocese of Albany, but the researcher should not assume a specific parish — search the diocesan/parish finding aid cited in the guide rather than guess.

The New York State Census of 1865 and 1875 each include a Marriage schedule (marriages in the 12 months before the census) browsable by county and town at FamilySearch — useful as a substitute near 1864/1865 and 1874/1875 only, not for earlier years.

Search adjoining Albany, Fulton, Hamilton, Montgomery, Rensselaer, Schenectady, Warren and Washington Counties as well, since Saratoga County borders all of them and an Irish immigrant family could have married or recorded events just across a county line.

No known history of courthouse record loss is reported for Saratoga County itself (per the FamilySearch Wiki county page), unlike several other NY counties (Albany, Niagara, Orange, Schoharie, Sullivan) that did lose records.

args.guideSection:
## Jurisdiction overview
- **Formed:** February 7, 1791, from Albany County (FamilySearch Wiki, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/Saratoga_County,_New_York_Genealogy)
- **County seat:** Ballston Spa
- **Parent jurisdiction:** New York, United States
- **Population during period:** 1850: 45,646; 1860: 51,729; 1870: 51,529 (a slight decline); 1880: 55,156 (FamilySearch Wiki county page)
- **Economy:** Agricultural towns plus the resort/spa industry at Saratoga Springs; the Champlain Canal (1823) and Erie Canal (1825) brought commerce and migration through the county.
- **Ethnic composition:** The wiki names no period-specific ethnic breakdown for this county; an Irish-born Catholic family (as in this case) would have been part of the mid-19th-century Irish immigration documented statewide, including the "US Famine Irish Passenger Index, 1846-1851."
- **Religious denominations:** Baptist, Episcopal, Methodist, Reformed Protestant Dutch, Society of Friends (Quaker), and Roman Catholic parishes under the Diocese of Albany (FamilySearch Wiki, Saratoga County Genealogy page, Church Records section).
- **Key historical events:** The Civil War (1861-1865) drew Saratoga County men into New York regiments and produced town soldier registers.

## Boundary changes
- Saratoga County was created from Albany County on 7 Feb 1791; no further boundary changes are noted for the 1855-1880 period (FamilySearch Wiki county page).
- Before 1791, any earlier records for this territory would be found under Albany County.

args.guideSection:
### Vital records (civil registration)
- **Start date:** Local (town/city/village) registration of marriages began in 1847 but compliance was weak and lapsed after a few years; statewide marriage registration did not begin until 1880 (FamilySearch Wiki, New York Vital Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_Vital_Records). Saratoga County's own page gives the same 1880 marriage date.
- **What exists:** For 1855-1864 (the likely marriage window), no civil marriage record is expected at the town, county or state level — this falls in the gap between the lapsed 1847 law and the 1880 statewide system.
- **Where held:** Any surviving town-clerk marriage records from 1847-1850 would be with the town clerk; post-1880 state registrations are with the town/village clerk and the NY State Department of Health.
- **Gaps:** The entire 1850-1880 period is a weak-registration era for marriages outside the brief 1847-1850 compliance window.
- **Pre-registration alternatives:** Church marriage registers, the 1865 and 1875 New York State Census marriage schedules, and newspaper marriage notices (below).

### Church records
- **Denominations present:** Baptist, Episcopal, Methodist Episcopal, Reformed Protestant Dutch, Society of Friends, and Roman Catholic (FamilySearch Wiki, Saratoga County Genealogy, Church Records section).
- **Record types:** Baptisms, marriages, burials; Quaker meetings also kept marriage and removal certificates.
- **Where held:** Digitized examples found by this survey (volume_search) include: Saratoga Reformed Dutch Protestant Church, Schuylerville, marriages 1790-1857 (image group 007767898_009_M98S-6Q6, 52% indexed, full-text searchable); First Presbyterian Church at Ballston, Ballston Center, marriages 1783-1865 (007767898_011_M98S-6QF, 52% indexed, full-text searchable); Presbyterian Church, Charlton, marriages 1801-1862 (007767898_012_M98S-6QN, 51% indexed, full-text searchable); Reformed Dutch Church of Amity, Vischer Ferry, marriages 1840-1855 (007767898_017_M98S-6QL, 34% indexed, full-text searchable). The NYGenWeb site also hosts free transcriptions: Old Reformed Dutch Church of Schuylerville marriages 1790-1857, and Schuylerville Methodist Episcopal Church marriages 1854-1869 (wiki_search result, Saratoga, Saratoga County, New York Genealogy page).
- **Gaps:** No Catholic parish register for Saratoga County in this period was returned by any tool in this survey; Saratoga County's Catholic parishes fall under the Diocese of Albany, but no tool result names which specific parish served the county's Irish Catholic population in 1855-1864 — this must be confirmed separately (e.g., via the diocesan or parish finding aid named below) rather than assumed.
- **Language:** The records found are in English.

### Census records
- **Federal/national census:** 1850, 1860, 1870, 1880 federal population census, all covering Saratoga County and listing households (1850 onward lists all household members; 1880 adds relationship to head of household).
- **State/provincial census:** New York State Census taken in 1855, 1865, and 1875 — all three fall inside or adjoin the target period (FamilySearch collections 1937366, 1491284, 1918735, each with millions of person records statewide).
- **Other enumerations:** The 1865 and 1875 New York State Census volumes each include a Marriage schedule and a Mortality schedule covering the 12 months before the census (ending 1 June); content includes husband's and wife's names, ages, prior marital status, and date/place of marriage.
- **Access:** Federal and state census years listed are indexed and imaged at FamilySearch and Ancestry; the marriage/mortality schedules require browsing to the end of the population schedule for the town, per FamilySearch Wiki instructions.

### Probate and court records
- **Types:** Wills, administrations, guardianships, inventories.
- **Testate or intestate:** Not yet known for Thomas Hanrahan; search both series.
- **Date range:** Surrogate Court probate from 1791; catalog_search found microfilmed will indexes 1799-1893 and wills 1905-1911 (e.g. catalog entries under image groups 005121426 and 005121425).
- **Where held:** Saratoga County Surrogate Court, Ballston Spa; also FamilySearch Library microfilm.

### Land records
- **Survey system:** Not detailed by tools consulted for this period.
- **Land-distribution jurisdiction:** County recorder of deeds (Saratoga County Clerk's office handles land records per the wiki county page).
- **Types:** Deeds, mortgages.
- **Date range:** From 1791 (county formation).
- **Where held:** Saratoga County Clerk's office; FamilySearch catalog lists additional land-record resources under the county's catalog subject page.

### Military records
- **Relevant conflicts:** American Civil War (1861-1865).
- **Record types:** Town clerks' Civil War service registers (full name, residence, birth date/place, parents' names, marital status, enlistment/discharge/death), service records, muster rolls.
- **Where held:** Originals at the New York State Archives, Albany; microfilm at FamilySearch Library (FS Library Film 1993401-37); indexed at Ancestry.

### Cemetery records
- **Major cemeteries:** Not itemized by tools for this specific period; the wiki county page links FindAGrave, BillionGraves, Interment.net, Names in Stone, New York Gravestones and the NYGenWeb cemetery list for the county.
- **Online coverage:** FindAGrave and BillionGraves searches by county are available via the links above; "New York, Cemetery Abstracts, 1800-1965" (FamilySearch collection 2552111, 251,828 people) covers the period.
- **Physical records:** Sexton/burial registers held locally; not itemized by tools in this survey.

### Newspaper records
- **Local papers:** The wiki names the Saratoga Sentinel (marriage/death notices indexed 1819-1837, so just before this period) and notes The Saratogian index begins only in 1999. For 1855-1880, the statewide "Barber Collection" newspaper marriage extracts (1801-1880, Ancestry collection 8936) and the "Index to Marriages and Deaths in the New York Herald" (1856-1863, Ancestry collection 49240) may carry notices for Saratoga County residents.
- **Where held:** Ancestry (subscription); FamilySearch Wiki page "Saratoga County, New York Genealogy," Newspapers section.
- **Content value:** Marriage/death notices, residence, newspaper of origin.

### Immigration/emigration records
- **Relevant ports:** New York City (nearest major port of entry for Irish immigrants reaching upstate New York).
- **Record types:** Passenger lists, naturalization records, alien declarations.
- **Where held:** "New York, County Naturalization Records, 1791-1980" (FamilySearch collection 1999177, index & images) and "US Famine Irish Passenger Index, 1846-1851" are relevant given Thomas Hanrahan's Irish birth; naturalization records for Saratoga County would be filed with the county court.
- **Content note:** Passenger lists list every person aboard, including children traveling with parents — review the full manifest, not just the named ancestor.

### Tax records
- **Types:** Property/personal tax assessments.
- **Date range:** Catalog_search found an 1840 Saratoga County assessment roll (koha:164757); no 1855-1880 assessment roll was returned by this survey.
- **Where held:** FamilySearch Library (microfilm/catalog); Saratoga County Clerk.
- **Substitute value:** Could help place the family in a specific town between census years, if located.

### Other record types
- Town registers (Civil War service), Quaker monthly-meeting minutes (1794-1862 Saratoga Monthly Meeting, Hicksite, and 1828-1846 Orthodox), and compiled genealogies/biographies (e.g., Hudson-Mohawk Genealogical and Family Memoirs) may mention Irish immigrant families only incidentally; of limited direct use for this Catholic family but worth checking for associates.

args.guideSection:
### Online repositories
| Repository | Collections for this place | Gap it fills | Access |
|---|---|---|---|
| FamilySearch | New York, State Census 1855/1865/1875 (collections 1937366, 1491284, 1918735); New York, Marriages 1686-1980 (1680847); New York, County Marriages 1778-1848/1908-1937 (1618491); New York, Church and Civil Marriages 1704-1995 (2373836); New York, County Naturalization Records 1791-1980 (1999177); digitized church volumes found by volume_search (image groups 007767898_009/011/012/017) | Fills the civil-marriage-record gap (no state marriage registration before 1880) with church marriage registers and census marriage schedules | Free |
| Ancestry | New York Marriage Notices 1800-1855 (collection 4244); New York Marriage Newspaper Extracts (Barber Collection) 1801-1880 (collection 8936); Index to Marriages and Deaths in the New York Herald 1856-1863 (collection 49240); New York State Census 1855/1865/1875 (collections 7181/7218/7250) | Fills the "Records NOT online" newspaper-notice gap for marriages in this period | Subscription |
| NYGenWeb (saratoganygenweb.com) | Marriages in the Old Reformed Dutch Church of Schuylerville, 1790-1857; Schuylerville Methodist Episcopal Church Marriages, 1854-1869 | Fills the gap left by the absence of Catholic parish registers online, for the two Protestant denominations transcribed here | Free |

**Coverage of this survey:** 185 digitized volumes matched Saratoga County for 1855-1880 across all record types; the summary call covered all 185 by record-type group, but only the first 10 full volume records were returned in this response (31 for Marriage alone are within the Marriage group: 25 volumes total, 11 browse-only, 8 full-text-only, with the remainder indexed+images or mixed). The FamilySearch Catalog search returned 340 total matches for Saratoga County; only the first 25 (10 fully hydrated) were examined here.

### Physical repositories
| Repository | Holdings | Access method |
|---|---|---|
| Saratoga County Courthouse, 30 McMaster St, Ballston Spa, NY 12020 | Marriage, divorce, court and land records (County Clerk); probate records (Surrogate Court) | In-person or by mail, phone 518-451-8840 |
| New York State Archives, Albany | Civil War town registers (originals), state-level indexes to birth/marriage/death certificates | In-person or online request |
| Saratoga Springs Public Library, 49 Henry Street, Saratoga Springs, NY 12866 | Local history and genealogical resources | Phone (518) 584-7860 |
| Saratoga County Historical Society / Brookside Museum, 6 Charlton Street, Ballston Spa | Surname files, local collections | Phone (518) 885-4000 |
| Diocese of Albany (Roman Catholic) | Parish sacramental registers for Catholic parishes in Saratoga County — specific parish for this family not identified by this survey | Contact diocesan archives directly |

## Records NOT online
- Civil marriage records before 1880 do not exist as a state-level series (registration did not begin until 1880), so there is no online civil marriage record to find for a 1855-1864 marriage.
- Many of the 185 digitized volumes located by this survey are browse-only images (e.g., the Saratoga Reformed Dutch Church and Ballston Presbyterian marriage volumes are only about half name-indexed) — the remaining unindexed portion must be browsed page by page.
- Catholic parish sacramental registers for this county were not found online by any tool in this survey.
- Saratoga County tax/assessment rolls for 1855-1880 were not located; only an 1840 roll was found in the catalog.

## Known record losses
- The FamilySearch Wiki county page states plainly: "There is no known history of courthouse disasters in this county" (Saratoga County, New York Genealogy, Record Loss section) — so no county-wide record loss is documented for Saratoga County itself, unlike several other New York counties (Albany, Niagara, Orange, Schoharie, Sullivan) named on the statewide Vital Records page as having record loss.
- No record loss specific to marriage registers was identified; the absence of civil marriage records before 1880 is a registration-coverage gap, not a loss.

## Research tips
- Civil marriage registration in New York did not begin statewide until 1880–1881, and the earlier 1847 local law saw compliance lapse within a few years, so a marriage in the 1855-1864 window must be sought in church records or census marriage schedules rather than a government marriage certificate (FamilySearch Wiki, New York Vital Records, https://www.familysearch.org/en/wiki/New_York_Vital_Records).
- The 1865 and 1875 New York State Census each carry a Marriage schedule for the 12 months before the census — useful only if the marriage falls near those dates, not for an earlier 1855-1864 marriage (FamilySearch Wiki, Saratoga County, New York Genealogy, Census Records section).
- If no marriage record turns up in Saratoga County, search the towns and surrounding counties, since couples often married where the bride lived or eloped elsewhere (FamilySearch Wiki, New York Vital Records, Strategy section).
- No tool result in this survey names the Catholic parish serving Saratoga County's Irish Catholic population in 1855-1864 — do not guess a specific parish; follow up with the Diocese of Albany or a dedicated parish-identification step before searching sacramental registers.
- Search adjoining Albany, Fulton, Hamilton, Montgomery, Rensselaer, Schenectady, Warren and Washington Counties as well as Saratoga, since the neighboring-counties table on the county's wiki page lists these as bordering jurisdictions.
- Review full passenger-manifest entries, not just the named individual, since infants and children travelling with parents are listed on the same line group.

  - Mary: born 17 Feb 1871 in Ireland. The Irish baptism entry names Thomas and Johanna Ryan as parents.
  - John: born 28 Nov 1872 at Ardfinnan, County Tipperary, Ireland. His baptism entry names the same parents.
  - Elizabeth (about 1869) and Thomas (about 1870): both recorded as born in New York City.

  - **Separate tree conflict:** John's and Mary's attached birth records disagree on birthplace. The project already flags this for conflict resolution.
  - **No marriage record before 1880:** per loc_001, New York State had no civil marriage registration before 1880, so none is expected at the state level.

  1. pli_001, fs_hints, FamilySearch: review pending hints on KHGX-XWG.

  4. pli_004, vital record, New York City, FamilySearch: NYC marriage records and the New York Marriages index. The two older children were born there around 1869-70.

  7. pli_007, church, Saratoga County, adjoining counties and the Diocese of Albany, FamilySearch: identify the Catholic parish first, because no tool named one and I did not guess. This is lower probability.

entry.jurisdiction: Ardfinnan, County Tipperary, Ireland (Catholic parish and neighbouring parishes)
entry.rationale: Survey finding that changes the premise: the tree's attached baptism entries record Mary born 17 Feb 1871 (Ireland) and John born 28 Nov 1872 at Ardfinnan, Tipperary, naming Thomas Hanrahan and Johanna Ryan as parents, while the 1880 census gives only Saratoga residence. Elizabeth (about 1869) and Thomas (about 1870) are recorded as born in New York City. So the family may have been in Ireland by 1871 and the marriage may be Irish, not Saratoga. Search name-searchable Ireland, Catholic Parish Registers, 1740-1900 and Ireland, Marriages, 1619-1898 for Thomas Hanrahan and Johanna Ryan (variants Hanrahan/Hanraghan/Hourihan/Hanran, Johanna/Hannah/Joanna/Ryan/Ryn). No Ireland locality survey exists yet; the orchestrator should run one for Ireland/Tipperary.

Irish civil registration of Catholic marriages began in 1864, so a marriage in Ireland from 1864 may be in Ireland, Civil Registration Indexes, 1845-1958 and Ireland, Civil Registration, 1845-1913 (both name-searchable); also the civil birth entries for Mary (1871) and John (1872) state the mother's maiden name. Fallback if the church register search finds no marriage. Registration-district assignment for Ardfinnan to be confirmed in the Ireland locality survey.

entry.jurisdiction: New York City, New York, United States
entry.rationale: Elizabeth (about 1869) and Thomas (about 1870) are recorded as born in New York City, so the couple lived there by 1869. loc_001 lists New York, New York City Marriage Records, 1829-1938 and New York, Marriages, 1686-1980 as name-searchable. Pre-1880 NYC marriage coverage is partial, so a miss is not a negative finding. The Saratoga guide's statement that civil marriage registration lapsed applies to Saratoga and the state; NYC kept city records.

entry.rationale: Place the couple between 1860 and 1880 to test where they lived at the likely marriage date: 1860 and 1870 US federal census, plus New York State Census 1865 and 1875 (loc_001: name-searchable). The 1865 and 1875 marriage schedules cover only the 12 months before each census, so browse the Saratoga town schedules for a marriage in 1864-65 or 1874-75 only. Children's stated birthplaces (Ireland versus New York) will clarify the migration sequence that conflicts in the tree.

Lower probability because the children's records suggest the family reached Saratoga after 1872.

entry.jurisdiction: New York, United States (Saratoga County town registers; NARA)
entry.rationale: A stone mason born about 1840 would be of Civil War age. If he served, the town Civil War registers and New York, Civil War Service Records of Union Soldiers, 1861-1865 (name-searchable) give residence and marital status, and any pension file (Thomas or widow Johanna, filed decades later) often states the marriage date and place. Window is sized to the pension series, not the 1860-1864 marriage window. Only pursue if a service record matches this Thomas by residence and birthplace.

Also New York, County Naturalization Records, 1791-1980 (name-searchable).

entry.identity_question: Is the Irish-baptised Mary (a_064) the 1880 census Mary (a_026, age 15, born New York) of the Saratoga household headed by Thomas Hanrahan?
entry.independence_analysis: The two records were made by different creators under different circumstances: the Irish entry was recorded at the event from the presenting parent, while the 1880 census was taken eight years later from an unnamed household member. They are not derivatives of one another, so they count as two sources. They are not fully independent on the parents' names, since the census household and the Irish entry both name Thomas Hanrahan and Johanna Ryan, but the Irish entry's names came from a different informant at a different time, so they corroborate the family link rather than repeat it. The birthplace claims are separate information items, each resting on its own informant.
entry.weighing_analysis: The decisive factor is age. The census gives Mary as 15 in June 1880, which places her birth around 1864-65. The Irish entry gives 17 February 1871, which would make her about nine at the census. A six-year gap is outside the one-to-two-year tolerance of census age estimates, so the census entry and the Irish entry cannot describe one child without one of them being badly wrong. Secondary factors: the census lists the four children in descending age order with Mary first, and an 1871 Mary would sit after Thomas (born about 1869-70) in that order. Also, no second Mary appears in the census, so an 1871 Mary would have had to die before June 1880. The Irish entry is the stronger record for the date and place it states, but it does not identify this census child.

fields.weighing_analysis: The decisive factor is age, now reinforced by a second record. The 1880 census gives Mary as 15 in June 1880, placing her birth around 1864-65. The New York State census of June 1865 lists a Mary Hanrahan as an infant in the household of Thomas Hanrahan and Joanna, independently fixing a Mary born by mid-1865 in that household. The Irish entry gives 17 February 1871, about six years later than both. Census age error is one to two years, so the two cannot describe one child. Secondary factors: the 1880 census lists the children in descending age order, and an 1871 Mary would fall after Thomas (about 1869-70), which the census order does not show. No second Mary appears in 1880, so an 1871 Mary would have had to die before June 1880 with no trace. The Irish entry is a strong record of the date and place it states, but it does not identify this household's child.
fields.resolution_rationale: The problem is whether the Mary baptised in Ireland in February 1871 is the Mary counted in the 1880 Saratoga household as fifteen and born in New York. It matters because the Irish entry would move this child, and the family's whereabouts, into Tipperary and bear on the marriage question. The 1880 census, taken from an unnamed household member, gives an 1864-65 New York birth. The June 1865 state census, taken by an enumerator at the dwelling, shows the same household with an infant Mary, which fixes the child's birth before mid-1865 and independently contradicts an 1871 birth. The Irish entry was given by the presenting parent near the event and names Thomas Hanrahan and Johanna Ryan, but the names are common in Tipperary, and the Irish family is probably a different couple (see the marriage conflict registered alongside this one). The Mary in the New York household is therefore most likely the subject's daughter, and the Irish Mary most likely belongs to another family. No single record proves that exclusion, because the Irish Mary has not been traced to her own household after 1871. The identity is therefore left open rather than resolved, with no preferred assertion. Records that would decide it: a Mary Hanrahan death between 1871 and 1880 in Tipperary or New York; a Tipperary parish entry showing the Ballylooby couple's household; and the 1870 federal census listing the household's children and their ages.

entry.description: Is the Thomam Hanrahan who married Johan Ryan at Ballylooby, County Tipperary, on 1 Feb 1868 (Ireland Catholic parish register, src_004) the Thomas Hanrahan who headed the Northumberland, Saratoga household in June 1865 with wife Joanna and an infant Mary (NY State Census 1865, src_006), and so the subject's husband?
entry.identity_question: Is the Ballylooby groom of 1 Feb 1868 (a_084) the same man as the Northumberland head of household in 1865 (a_132, a_137), who already had a wife and infant in New York?
entry.independence_analysis: The Ballylooby entry was recorded by the parish from the parties themselves at the marriage in Ireland; the 1865 census was recorded by an enumerator at the dwelling, with the household's answers from an unnamed member. The two are different creators and different events, so they are independent. The 1865 entry adds no marriage date of its own: it shows a husband and wife with a child already in the household, which implies a marriage before about 1864. That implication rests on the household composition, not on a stated marriage, so it is a separate information item from the Ballylooby entry. The Northumberland household also shows Thomas Hanrahan, Irish-born, in the 1860 census with his mother Margaret at age twenty. That earlier record is not a source for the marriage but bears on whether the 1865 head is the subject.
entry.weighing_analysis: The decisive factor is positive placement of the 1865 head. In 1860 the Northumberland household of Margaret Hanrahan, widow, includes Thomas Hanrahan, Irish-born, age 20, in the same township. In 1865 the same township shows Thomas Hanrahan, Irish-born, age 22, with wife Joanna and infant Mary. In 1880 the Saratoga household shows Thomas, Irish-born, age 40, with Johannah and a Mary of 15 born in New York. The two-year age difference between 1860 and 1865 is within ordinary census age error, so the 1865 head is most likely the subject. If he is the subject, he had a wife and an infant in New York by June 1865, so the Ballylooby marriage of February 1868 cannot be his first marriage. The Ballylooby record names a groom and bride with the surname and the bride's short given name only, with no parents or residence, so it carries nothing to tie the groom to Saratoga. The likeliest explanation is a second Thomas Hanrahan and Johan Ryan in Tipperary, which the Irish baptisms of 1871 and 1872 in the same county also suggest.
entry.resolution_rationale: The problem is whether the Tipperary marriage of 1868 is the subject's marriage. It matters because the answer sets when and where the subject married Johanna Ryan. The 1868 Ballylooby entry, a parish record from Ireland, gives a groom named Thomam Hanrahan and a bride named Johan Ryan. The 1865 New York census, taken by an enumerator at the dwelling, shows a Thomas Hanrahan, Irish-born, with a wife Joanna and an infant Mary already in the household in Northumberland, Saratoga County. The 1860 census of the same township places a Thomas Hanrahan, Irish-born and about twenty, in his mother's household there, which links the 1865 head to the subject. The 1865 head is most likely the subject, and a man already married with a child in New York in June 1865 cannot have married in Tipperary in February 1868 as a first marriage. The 1868 record is therefore most likely a different couple of the same names, a common pairing in Tipperary. The discrepancy is explained by the commonness of the names and by the census and parish records being taken for different households. The identity is not resolved because the 1868 entry itself lacks any link to Saratoga, and no record yet shows the Ballylooby couple in America or the subject in Ireland in 1868. Records that would decide it: a New York State census marriage schedule for Northumberland (June 1864 to June 1865), a Catholic register entry for the subject's marriage in Saratoga County or adjoining counties, and an 1870 or 1875 census entry for Johanna Ryan's birthplace and marriage date.

EVIDENCE SUMMARY:

Positive evidence:
- 1860 US Census (src_005): Thomas Hanrahan, age 20, born Ireland, in Northumberland, Saratoga County, NY — a good fit for the subject
- 1865 NY State Census (src_006): Thomas Hanrahan (head, age 22) and Joanna Hanrahan (wife, age 19) already married, with infant Mary, in Northumberland, Saratoga County — speculative link to subject, but the same township as the 1860 and 1880 records; places the marriage before mid-1865
- 1880 US Census (src_001): Thomas and Johannah Hanrahan in Saratoga, married, with four children all born in New York (supporting the conclusion the family was in New York, not Ireland, through the 1860s-1870s — though two Irish baptism records complicate this)

Complicating records (may not belong to this family):
- Ireland Births and Baptisms (src_002): Mary Hanrahan born 17 Feb 1871 in Ireland to Thomas Hanrahan and Johanna Ryan — conflict-resolution says this is probably a different family, since the 1865 Saratoga census already shows an infant Mary in this couple's household
- Ireland Births and Baptisms (src_003): John Hanrahan born 28 Nov 1872, Ardfinnan, Tipperary, to Thomas Hanrahan and Johanna Ryan — conflict c_002 was resolved in favor of this record being correct, but conflict-resolution (wrap-up) suggests this too may belong to a different Tipperary family given the 1865 New York evidence
- Catholic parish marriage (src_004): Thomam Hanrahan / Johan Ryan, 1 Feb 1868, Ballylooby, County Tipperary — conflict c_003 (new) says this is probably a different couple, since the 1865 Saratoga census shows Thomas and Joanna already married there

FINDING from conflict-resolution: The marriage most likely took place around 1862–1864, probably in or near Saratoga County, New York. The 1865 NY State Census is the strongest single piece of evidence for the marriage having occurred before mid-1865.

NOT SEARCHED: 1870 census, Catholic church records for Saratoga/Albany diocese, Civil War service records, naturalization records, death/burial records, NARA pension files, newspaper notices.

Please write the conclusion at the appropriate tier (probably "Possible" given the indirect evidence and unresolved conflicts), encode the marriage date range in the tree if warranted, and mark the question resolved.

entry.narrative_markdown:
**Question.** When and where did Thomas Hanrahan, born about 1840 in Ireland and living in Saratoga, New York, in 1880, marry Johanna Ryan?

**Conclusion: not proved, and the question stays open.** Two identity conflicts that bear directly on whether the records describe the subject's family remain unresolved, so the sources cannot yet be correlated into a marriage date and place. No marriage is asserted in the tree.

**What the records show.** The 1880 US Census lists Thomas and Johannah Hanrahan in Saratoga, New York, married, with four children ("United States, Census, 1880", FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:MZF2-Y55)). The 1860 US Census lists a Thomas Hanrahan, Irish-born, age 20, in the Northumberland, Saratoga County household of Margaret Hanrahan ("United States, Census, 1860", FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:MC4N-WK2)). The 1865 New York State Census lists Thomas Hanrahan, age 22, with wife Joanna, and an infant Mary in Northumberland ("New York, State Census, 1865", FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:QVNN-7MNR)). All three are derivative index entries; the census informants are unnamed household members, so the information is of indeterminate quality, apart from the enumerator's own record of the household's presence in place and year. The 1865 entry states no marriage date. A wife and infant imply a marriage before about 1864, but that is an inference, and linking the 1865 head to the 1860 son and the 1880 head rests on name, township and a two-year age drift, not on any record that names all three.

**Competing Irish records.** A Catholic parish entry records Thomam Hanrahan and Johan Ryan marrying on 1 Feb 1868 at Ballylooby, County Tipperary ("Ireland, Catholic Parish Registers, 1740-1900", FamilySearch (https://www.familysearch.org/ark:/61903/1:1:6267-W22Q : Thu Nov 21 12:34:58 UTC 2024)). Two Irish baptisms name Thomas Hanrahan and Johanna Ryan as parents of Mary (1871) and John (Ardfinnan, 1872) ("Ireland, Births and Baptisms, 1620-1881", FamilySearch, entries of 1871 and 1872). These are derivative index entries whose parents' names came from the presenting parties, so they are good evidence of what they state, but they carry no residence or parentage linking the couple to Saratoga.

**Why the correlation is blocked.** If the 1865 Northumberland head is the subject, he was already married with a child in New York three years before the Ballylooby marriage, so that marriage would belong to a different couple of common Tipperary names. The age of Mary (about 15 in 1880, an infant in 1865) also does not fit the 1871 Irish Mary. Conflict-resolution has weighed this and leans toward the New York reading, but it deliberately left both identity questions unresolved: the Irish Mary against the 1880 Mary (c_001), and the Ballylooby groom against the 1865 head (c_003). A third question, whether the 1872 John is the 1880 census John (c_002), was resolved in favor of the Irish baptism, which pulls the other way, since it would put the couple in Tipperary in 1872 and sits uneasily with the New York reading. Because these conflicts concern whether the sources describe one man and one family, the records cannot validly be combined yet.

**Provisional lean, not a conclusion.** The best-supported working hypothesis is a marriage before mid-1865, probably in or near Saratoga County, about 1862 to 1864. It is not encoded in the tree: it is an inference from household composition, and the Ballylooby entry and the 1872 baptism remain unexplained.

**What would settle it.** The 1865 NY State Census marriage schedule for Northumberland; a Catholic register entry in Saratoga or adjoining counties (Albany diocese); the 1870 federal census and 1875 NY State Census for Johanna's birthplace and the children's ages and birthplaces; and records of a Mary death 1871 to 1880. Unresolved identity conflicts c_001 and c_003 should go back to conflict-resolution once any of these is searched.

We now have a foundation for the research. Thomas and Johanna's children were all born in New York, with the eldest Mary arriving around 1864–1865, which puts the wedding most likely between 1858 and 1864. Because New York did not require civil marriage registration until 1880, the most promising leads are Catholic parish records from the Albany diocese, the 1865 and 1875 New York state censuses (which included marriage lists), and FamilySearch's indexed collections of New York marriage records. The next step is laying out exactly which record sets to search and in what order.

Continue with `planning the searches`?

The research plan is set. We will search Irish Catholic parish and civil records for County Tipperary first — because two of the children's baptism records place the family in Ardfinnan, Tipperary in 1871 and 1872, making an Irish marriage very likely — then New York City marriage records (where two older children appear to have been born), state and federal censuses, and later death records that might name a marriage date and place. Before searching, though, the records already on file disagree about where Mary and John Hanrahan were born: the 1880 census says New York, while their baptism records say Ireland. That conflict needs to be sorted out first because it determines whether we are looking for an Irish or an American marriage.

One conflict is settled and one remains open. The 1880 census entry saying John Hanrahan was born in New York has been outweighed by his Irish baptism record — made close to the event by the presenting parent — which names the same Thomas Hanrahan and Johanna Ryan and places his birth in Ardfinnan, County Tipperary, in November 1872. That means the family was in Tipperary at that point, making an Irish marriage more likely. The question of Mary's birth is still open: the baptism record gives her birth as February 1871, but the 1880 census puts her age at 15, which would mean she was born around 1864–65 — a gap too large to be a simple error, suggesting these may be two different children, or one record is significantly wrong. The next step is checking the hints already attached to Thomas in the family tree, which may surface a marriage record or other evidence.

The searches have turned up three important new records. The most striking is the 1865 New York State Census, which shows Thomas and Joanna Hanrahan already married and living in Northumberland, Saratoga County with an infant daughter Mary — placing the marriage before mid-1865, three years before the Catholic parish record from Ballylooby, County Tipperary dated 1 February 1868. That conflict needs careful attention: either the 1865 couple is a different Thomas and Joanna, or the Ballylooby 1868 record is a different couple with the same names. The 1860 census also places a Thomas Hanrahan, age 20, born in Ireland, in the same Northumberland township, living in what appears to be a family of origin household — a good fit for the subject. Research is wrapped up. Here is where things stand.

The best evidence for when and where Thomas Hanrahan and Johanna Ryan married is the 1865 New York State Census, which found Thomas and Joanna Hanrahan already living as husband and wife with an infant daughter in Northumberland, Saratoga County — the same township where Thomas appears as a 20-year-old in 1860 and where the whole family lives in 1880. That places the marriage before mid-1865, most likely around 1862 to 1864, and probably in or near Saratoga County. A Catholic parish marriage record from Ballylooby, County Tipperary dated 1 February 1868 names a Thomam Hanrahan and Johan Ryan, but the conflict-resolution work concluded that this is probably a different couple, since the subject was already married in New York three years earlier.

Two conflicts in the evidence could not be fully resolved with what was searched. One concerns a Mary Hanrahan whose baptism is recorded in Ireland in 1871 — the age gap with the 1880 census Mary is too large for the same child, suggesting the Irish baptism belongs to a different family. The other is about whether the 1865 Saratoga couple and the 1868 Tipperary couple are the same people; the evidence now leans toward no, but the question cannot be closed without the 1865 census marriage schedule for Northumberland, local Catholic registers for the Albany diocese, and the 1870 census. Those searches were blocked by a connection problem with FamilySearch and could not be run. Pension files at the National Archives and newspaper archives on Ancestry were set up as links for you to check at any time — if Thomas or his widow Johanna filed a pension, it very likely states the exact marriage date and place.

The conclusion is recorded as not yet proved: a probable marriage before mid-1865 near Saratoga County, New York, with the supporting searches still incomplete.
